tasks.q: How does an operating system multitask on a single core?
a: It switches between programs very quickly, giving each a small slice of processor time
It runs every program at exactly the same moment
It uses the graphics card instead
tasks.fb: Each program gets a few milliseconds, then the OS moves on.

a: A program that is currently running, with its own place in memory
tasks.fb: A program on disk becomes a process when it is loaded and run.

tasks.q: Put these steps of a context switch in order.
steps: A process runs until its time slice ends
The OS saves the state of that process
The OS loads the saved state of the next process
The next process runs until its time slice ends
tasks.fb: Switching costs a little time itself, which is why too many open programs slows everything down.

tasks.q: Why might a video call be given a higher priority than a backup?
a: The call must keep up in real time, while the backup can wait
tasks.fb: Priority decides who gets the processor sooner, not how fast it runs.

tasks.q: Open all five programs. RAM has 8 blocks: put what fits into RAM, and the rest into virtual memory.
tasks.fb: The OS always uses RAM first, because it is far faster than the disk.

tasks.q: Why does the OS keep each process in its own area of memory?
a: So one program can't read or overwrite another program's data
tasks.fb: It's protection as well as organisation.

tasks.q: RAM now has only 5 blocks. Load the same programs sensibly.
tasks.fb: With less RAM, more has to live on the disk, and the machine feels slower.

tasks.q: What is the best fix for a computer constantly using virtual memory?
What does a device driver do?
a: Translates between the operating system and a particular piece of hardware
tasks.fb: It is the translator for that one device.

tasks.q: A new printer prints, but none of its extra features work. What is the most likely cause?
a: The OS is using a basic driver rather than the manufacturer's own
The printer is out of paper
tasks.fb: Generic drivers cover the basics only.

tasks.q: What does plug and play mean?
a: The operating system detects a new device and sets up its driver automatically
tasks.fb: It saves the user finding and installing a driver by hand.

tasks.q: Why can a bad driver crash the whole computer?
a: Drivers run with high privileges, close to the hardware
tasks.fb: A mistake there affects everything, not just one program.

tasks.q: Load these six programs. RAM has 8 blocks.
tasks.fb: Only what doesn't fit belongs in virtual memory.

tasks.q: Which part of the operating system is each job?
items: Giving each process a time slice
Choosing where a program sits in RAM
Swapping unused data out to disk
Loading a driver for a new printer
Sending data to the graphics card
tasks.fb: Three of the OS's jobs, all happening at once, all the time.

info.title: Milliseconds
info.text: A typical time slice is a few milliseconds. In the time it takes to blink, a processor may have switched between programs a hundred times.

info.title: Task manager
info.text: Open the task manager on any computer and you'll see dozens of processes running that you never started. Most belong to the operating system.

info.title: Thrashing
info.text: If RAM is so full that the OS spends more time swapping than working, it's called thrashing. The disk light stays on and nothing happens.

info.title: Cores help
info.text: A four-core processor really can run four things at once, and the OS still time slices on top of that, which is why a modern machine copes with so much.

info.title: Driver disks
info.text: Hardware used to come with a driver disk in the box. Now the OS downloads drivers automatically, which is why a new mouse works the moment you plug it in.

info.title: Blue screens
info.text: Most famous crash screens are caused by drivers rather than by the operating system itself, because drivers run with the deepest access to the hardware.
